source_text: Ἔτι δὲ καὶ τῶν λεγόντων μὴ ἀνίστασθαι τὴν σάρκα οἱ μὲν ὡς ἀδύνατον ἀναστῆναι λέγουσιν, οἱ δὲ ὡς μὴ προσῆκον τῷ θεῷ τὸ ἀνιστάνειν αὐτὴν διὰ τὸ εὐτελὲς καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητον αὐτῆς, οἱ δὲ ὅτι τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδὲ ἐπαγγελίαν ἔχειν. Πρῶτον οὖν δοκεῖ μέν μοι πρὸς τοὺς ἀδύνατον εἶναι λέγοντας τῷ θεῷ τὸ ταύτην ἀναστῆσαι διεξελθεῖν, ὅτι ἀγνοοῦσιν αὐτοὶ τῷ λόγῳ λέγοντες ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι πιστούς, καὶ διὰ τῶν ἔργων ἀποδεικνύντες ἀπίστους ἑαυτοὺς καὶ τῶν ἀπίστων ἀπιστοτέρους. Τῶν γὰρ ἐθνῶν ἁπάντων ἐπὶ τὰ εἴδωλα πεπιστευκότων καὶ πεπεισμένων ὅτι πάντα δυνατὰ τούτοις ἐστίν, ὡς καὶ Ὅμηρος, ὁ ποιητὴς αὐτῶν, φησίν· Θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα δύνανται Καὶ ·εῖα– (ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ·εῖα προσέθηκεν, ὅπερ ἐστὶν εὐχερῶς, ἵνα τὴν μεγαλειότητα τῆς τῶν θεῶν δυνάμεως ἐμφάνῃ), πολὺ οὖν τούτων ἀπιστότεροι φαίνονται. Eἰ γὰρ τοῖς εἰδώλοις τὰ ἔθνη, τοῖς θεοῖς αὐτῶν, οἳ ὦτα ἔχουσι καὶ οὐκ ἀκούουσιν, ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχουσι καὶ οὐκ ὄψονται, τὸ πάντα δύνασθαι πεπιστεύκασι, δαιμονίοις οὖσι, καθὼς ἡ γραφὴ λέγει, ὅτι Oἱ θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν δαιμόνια, πολὺ μᾶλλον ἡμεῖς, οἱ τὴν ἐξαίρετον καὶ ἀληθῆ πίστιν ἔχοντες, ὀφείλομεν τῷ θεῷ ἡμῶν πιστεύειν, ἔχοντες τεκμήρια· καὶ πρῶτον μὲν τὴν τοῦ πρωτοπλάστου γένεσιν, ὅτι ἐκ γῆς ὑπὸ θεοῦ γέγονεν· ἱκανὸν γὰρ τοῦτο δεῖγμα τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ δυνάμεως. Ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὴν μετὰ ταῦτα ἐξ ἀλλήλων γένεσιν κατανοοῦσιν ἔστιν ἰδεῖν, καὶ θαυμάσαι μειζόνως, ὅτι ἐξ ἐλαχίστης ·ανίδος ὑγροῦ τηλικοῦτον πλάσσεται ζῶον. Καίτοι γε εἰ ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ καὶ τοῦτο ἦν καὶ μὴ ἐφαίνετο γινόμενον, πολὺ τῶν ἄλλων ἦν ἀπιστότερον· ἀλλὰ γὰρ πιστότερον αὐτὸ ποιεῖ τὸ ἀποτέλεσμα. Ἀλλὰ μὴν περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἡμῖν ἔδειξεν ὁ σωτὴρ ἀποτελέσματα, ἃ μετ' ὀλίγον ἐροῦμεν. Νῦν δὲ τὸ δυνατὴν εἶναι τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν ἐπιδεικνύομεν, συγγνώμην αἰτούμενοι παρὰ τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας τέκνων, εἰ καὶ τῶν ἔξωθεν εἶναι δοκούντων καὶ κοσμικῶν λόγων ἁπτόμεθα· πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι οὐδέν ἐστιν ἔξωθεν τοῦ θεοῦ, οὐδὲ αὐτὸς ὁ κόσμος· ποίημα γάρ ἐστιν αὐτοῦ· δεύτερον ὅτι πρὸς ἀπίστους τούτους ποιούμεθα τοὺς λόγους. Eἰ γὰρ πρὸς πιστούς, αὐταρκὲς ἦν ἀποκρίνεσθαι τὸ ὅτι πεπιστεύκαμεν· νῦν δὲ διὰ ἀποδείξεων χωρεῖν ἀναγκαῖον. Ἱκανὰ μὲν οὖν καὶ τὰ προειρημένα τεκμήρια πρὸς τὸ δυνατὴν εἶναι δεικνύειν τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν· ἀλλ', ἐπεὶ λίαν εἰσὶν ἄπιστοι, καὶ ἀναγκαστικώτερον ἐπάξομεν τὸν λόγον, οὐκ ἐκ τῆς πίστεως, ὅτι μὴ τυγχάνουσιν ὄντες αὐτῆς, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς ἀπιστίας, τῆς μητρὸς αὐτῶν, λέγω δὴ τῶν κοσμικῶν λόγων. Eἰ γὰρ ἐκ τούτων ἐπιδεικνύομεν αὐτοῖς δυνατὴν εἶναι τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν, πολλῆς δήπουθεν αἰσχύνης εἰσὶν ἄξιοι, εἰ μήτε τοῖς τῆς πίστεως μήτε τοῖς τοῦ κόσμου ἀκολουθεῖν δύνανται.
pass_a_gloss: And yet also of those saying the flesh does not rise, some say it is impossible for it to rise, others that it is not fitting for God to raise it because of its worthlessness and contemptibility, and others that it has neither beginning nor promise. First, then, it seems to me to go through with those saying it is impossible for God to raise it, that they are ignorant, saying they are faithful by the word, and through deeds they demonstrate themselves unfaithful and more unfaithful than the unfaithful. For all the nations, having believed in idols and having been persuaded that all things are possible for them, as also Homer, their poet, says: 'The gods can do all things, and easily', (but he also added 'easily', which is 'eukheros', in order to show the greatness of the power of the gods), they appear much more unfaithful than these. For if the nations have believed in idols, their gods, who have ears and do not hear, and eyes and do not see, that they can do all things, being demons, as the scripture says, that 'The gods of the nations are demons', much more should we, who have the exceptional and true faith, owe it to our God to believe, having proofs; and first, the creation of the first-formed, that he was made from earth by God; for this is a sufficient example of God's power. And yet also, considering the generation from each other after these things, it is possible to see and marvel even more, that from a small drop of moist seed such a large living being is formed. And indeed, if this were in promise and not apparent, it would be more unfaithful than the others; but the outcome makes it more faithful. But our Savior has shown us the outcomes of the resurrection, which we will speak of shortly. Now, however, we demonstrate that the resurrection of the flesh is possible, asking forgiveness from the children of truth, if we also touch on external and worldly words; first, because nothing is outside of God, nor is the world itself, for it is his creation; second, because we make these words for the unfaithful. For if we were speaking to the faithful, it would be enough to answer that we have believed; now, however, it is necessary to proceed through demonstrations. The previously mentioned proofs are sufficient to show that the resurrection of the flesh is possible; but since they are very unfaithful, we will also bring a more necessary word, not from faith, because they do not have it, but from unfaithfulness, their mother, I mean the worldly words. For if we demonstrate to them from these that the resurrection of the flesh is possible, they are certainly worthy of much shame, if they are unable to follow either the things of faith or the things of the world.

bible_refs.note: The gods of the nations are demons

pass_b_english: Some who deny the resurrection of the flesh say it is impossible for it to rise; others claim it is not fitting for God to raise it because of its worthlessness and contemptibility; and still others argue that it has neither beginning nor promise. I think we should first engage with those who say it is impossible for God to raise it, because they are ignorant: they claim by word to be faithful, yet by their deeds they prove themselves unfaithful and even more unfaithful than the faithless. All the nations have believed in idols and have been persuaded that all things are possible for them, just as Homer, their poet, declares: 'The gods can do all things, and easily' (he added 'easily'—that is, *eukherōs*—to display the greatness of the gods' power). Yet these deniers appear far more unfaithful than the pagans. For if the nations have believed of their idols, their gods—who have ears but do not hear, eyes but do not see—that they can do all things, even though those gods are demons, as Scripture says, 'The gods of the nations are demons' (Psalm 96:5), then how much more ought we, who possess the exceptional and true faith, to trust our God, since we have proofs? First, there is the creation of the first-formed man, who was made from earth by God; this alone is a sufficient demonstration of God's power. Moreover, by observing the generation that follows from one another, we can see and marvel even more: from a tiny drop of moist seed such a vast living being is shaped. And indeed, if this came to pass only by promise and were not visibly occurring, it would be more unbelievable than anything else; but the result makes it more credible. Besides, our Savior has shown us the outcomes of the resurrection, which we will discuss shortly. For now, we demonstrate that the resurrection of the flesh is possible, asking pardon from the children of truth if we also appeal to arguments that seem external and worldly: first, because nothing lies outside God, not even the world itself, for it is His creation; second, because we address these arguments to the faithless. If we were speaking to the faithful, it would be enough to answer that we have believed; but now we must proceed through demonstrations. The proofs already mentioned are sufficient to show that the resurrection of the flesh is possible; yet because they are extremely faithless, we will bring a more compelling argument—not from faith, since they lack it, but from their own unfaithfulness, their mother, I mean worldly reasoning. For if we prove to them from these very sources that the resurrection of the flesh is possible, they deserve great shame if they can follow neither the things of faith nor the things of the world.
